items.title: Sympathetic vs. Parasympathetic
items.content: **Autonomic divisions:** Sympathetic pathways often mobilize cardiovascular and metabolic resources; parasympathetic pathways often support restoration, digestion, and energy conservation. The gas-versus-brake analogy is limited: both divisions can be active together, effects are organ-specific, and digestion is modulated rather than simply stopped. Use the cue for broad pathway recognition, not diagnosis or treatment.

items.title: Sleep Stages
items.content: **N1, N2, N3, REM:** N1 is light transitional sleep; N2 includes sleep spindles and K-complexes; N3 contains high-amplitude slow waves; REM commonly combines rapid eye movements, low skeletal-muscle tone, and wake-like mixed-frequency EEG. Cycles and proportions vary by age, health, medication, person, and night; dreaming and memory processing are not exclusive to REM.

items.title: Psychotropic Drug Classes
items.content: **Medication-class cue:** Antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood-stabilizing agents, anxiolytics, and stimulants are broad families with overlapping indications and agent-specific risks. A class name does not select a drug or predict response. Current labeling, interactions, age, pregnancy, health conditions, prior response, preference, monitoring, and qualified prescribing govern individual decisions.

items.title: Brain Imaging Techniques
items.content: **Structure versus function:** CT uses x-rays and is useful for rapid structural assessment; MRI uses magnetic fields and radiofrequency signals for detailed structure; fMRI infers activity from blood-oxygen changes; PET uses radiotracers to estimate molecular or metabolic processes; EEG records scalp electrical potentials with high temporal resolution. Each method has distinct resolution, artifacts, contraindications, and inferential limits.

items.title: Endocrine System & Hormones
items.content: **Endocrine cue:** The hypothalamus and pituitary coordinate many hormonal axes; thyroid hormones influence metabolism; adrenal cortex and medulla have different outputs; pancreatic hormones regulate glucose; gonadal hormones have reproductive and broader effects. Symptoms are nonspecific, feedback loops matter, and "master gland" or "bonding hormone" labels oversimplify distributed regulation. Medical testing is required for endocrine conclusions.

items.title: Neuron Structure
items.content: **Canonical neuron flow:** Dendrites and soma commonly receive and integrate inputs; axons propagate action potentials toward terminals; chemical synapses often release neurotransmitter onto receptors. This is not an always-one-way law: neurons receive inputs at multiple sites, electrical synapses may be bidirectional, and modulatory and retrograde signals occur. More dendrites do not translate mechanically into "more learning."

items.title: Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome
items.content: **GAS as historical model:** Alarm, resistance, and exhaustion describe Selye's broad account of prolonged physiological adaptation to demand. Real stress responses are dynamic and shaped by appraisal, controllability, duration, health, context, and resources; people do not inevitably pass through three discrete stages. "Exhaustion" is not a diagnosis, and the model does not by itself identify a stressor or intervention.

items.title: Consciousness & Altered States
items.content: **State cue:** Wakefulness, NREM sleep, REM sleep, sedation, and other altered states differ across behavioral responsiveness and multiple neural measures. Consciousness is not captured by one EEG rhythm, and hypnosis, meditation, substances, illness, and sleep are not interchangeable mechanisms. Separate subjective report, task performance, physiology, dose, context, and clinical status before drawing conclusions.

items.title: Brain Lobes & Functions
items.content: **Lobe map with limits:** Frontal regions contribute to motor control and executive functions; parietal regions to somatosensory and spatial processing; temporal regions to auditory, memory, and language networks; occipital regions to vision. Functions arise from distributed networks, vary within lobes, and can reorganize. A symptom or personality style cannot be localized from this mnemonic alone.

items.title: Aphasia Types
items.content: **Aphasia profiles:** Nonfluent and fluent labels describe patterns across speech production, comprehension, repetition, naming, reading, and writing. Broca- and Wernicke-type prototypes are useful contrasts, but individual lesions and profiles vary and do not map perfectly to one cortical spot. Aphasia is a language disorder, not loss of intelligence; assessment must examine the person's actual modalities and causes.

items.title: Sleep Stages
items.content: **Stage-recognition cue:** N1 marks transition into sleep; N2 is identified by spindles and K-complexes; N3 by slow-wave activity; REM by characteristic eye movements, low muscle tone, and mixed-frequency EEG. "Deep equals delta" can aid recall, but fixed 90-minute cycles and universal percentages are not rules. Age, timing, disorders, substances, and scoring methods alter architecture.

items.title: Split-Brain Research
items.content: **Hemispheric specialization:** In carefully tested people whose corpus callosum had been surgically sectioned, information restricted to one visual field could reveal differences in language report and visuospatial response. These findings concern task-specific lateralization and interhemispheric transfer. They do not support "logical left-brained" versus "creative right-brained" personality types or imply independent minds in ordinary brains.

items.title: Endocrine System & Hormones
items.content: **Hormone-axis cue:** Hypothalamic signals regulate pituitary outputs that influence thyroid, adrenal, gonadal, growth, lactation, and water-balance systems. Cortisol, oxytocin, melatonin, and catecholamines have context-, receptor-, and timing-dependent effects; none is simply a "stress," "bonding," or "sleep" chemical. Psychological symptoms may warrant medical consideration, but no symptom list establishes endocrine disease.
